google-forms.name: Google Forms
google-forms.tagline: A form collects answers. An event needs places counted, a ticket sent and a list that works at the door.
google-forms.meta_title: Replace Google Forms for Event Registration | Event Schedule
google-forms.description: How events really run on Google Forms, where the form stops, and what changes when a sign-up counts places, sends a QR ticket and scans at the door.
google-forms.keywords: Google Forms alternative for events, Google Forms replacement, event registration form, event signup form
google-forms.audience_hint: For organizers whose sign-up is a Google Form, a linked Sheet and a mail merge the night before.
google-forms.about: Google Forms is the form builder in Google Workspace: questions on a page, answers in a Responses tab and, if you link one, a Google Sheet. For events it is the default sign-up tool because everyone has filled one in and a form for a workshop or a potluck is ready in ten minutes. It collects answers. What happens to a place, a payment or a door list after Submit is yours to arrange.
google-forms.pricing_note: Google Forms is free, but payments and tickets have to come from other tools. Event Schedule does free registration, confirmation emails and door check-in on its free plan; paid tickets, at zero platform fees, are on Pro at $5/month.

tool_strengths: Many question types, from short answer to file upload, and sections that show or hide depending on an answer
Responses land in a linked Google Sheet as they arrive, ready to sort, filter and share with a co-organizer
Guests have filled one in before, and need no Google account unless you limit the form to one response or ask for a file
A form can close itself on a date or after a set number of responses
keep_when: what you are collecting is answers, not places: a volunteer skills survey, a menu vote, a call for speakers
the form needs many questions that branch, a file upload or a quiz score
the event is inside a school or company on Google Workspace, the form is limited to your own domain, and nobody needs a ticket
pain_points: The response limit counts submissions. One answer that says "me plus three" uses one of your 40 responses and four of your 40 chairs.
Someone emails on Thursday to say they cannot come. The form stays closed at its limit, and the person who found it full on Tuesday never hears that a place opened.
The receipt Google sends is a copy of the answers, and Google warns that it may not arrive. Guests write to ask whether they are in.
Payment lives in another tab. You paste a payment link into the description, then match names in the payment app against rows in the Sheet.
At the door the list is a printed Sheet. Finding Katherine, who registered as Kate, holds up the line, and nothing stops the same row being ticked twice.
The form link is not the event. The date, the address, parking and the poster live in a message somewhere else, and the form looks the same with five places left as with fifty.
google-forms.gaps_lead: Forms does what it says: it asks and it stores. These are the moments in an event's life when asking and storing is not enough.
google-forms.gaps_close: For a sign-up where being a row in a Sheet is the whole point, none of this matters, and Forms is the right amount of tool.

today.title: An event on Google Forms, start to finish
today.intro: This is the usual routine for a free workshop with 40 places and an optional paid lunch. Each step works. The effort is in the joins between them.

steps.title: Build the form
steps.description: Name, email, number of guests, dietary needs. You turn on Collect email addresses and choose Responder input so people without a Google account can sign up, then write a confirmation message that says "You are registered" before you know whether there will be room.

steps.title: Link the Sheet
steps.description: On the Responses tab you press Link to Sheets. Every submission becomes a row, and that Sheet is now your attendee list, your waitlist and your door list at once.

steps.title: Cap the places
steps.description: You set a response limit of 40 so the form closes itself. It counts submissions, not people, so you either drop the guests question or add up the column yourself and close the form early.

steps.title: Confirm and remind
steps.description: Send responders a copy of their response gives each person their answers back, if it clears their spam filter. The real confirmation, with the address and the time, is a mail merge from the Sheet. So is the reminder two days before.

steps.title: Take the money
steps.description: Forms has no payment question. The lunch fee is a payment link in the form description, and afterwards you compare the payment app's list with the Sheet and fill in a Paid column.

steps.title: Run the door
steps.description: You sort the Sheet by name, print it and tick people off. Cancellations that came by email are crossed out by hand, and you decide on the spot whether a walk-in can have the place.

today.outro: That is four tools and three manual joins: form to Sheet, Sheet to mail merge, Sheet to payment list. It holds for one event of 40. It gets heavy at the second date, the second ticket price or the first full house.

google-forms.native_lead: The same sign-up, where the form, the count, the confirmation and the door list are one record instead of four.

es_solutions.title: A Register button that counts places
es_solutions.description: Switch an event to Free registration and its page gets a Register button that asks for a name and an email, and a phone number if you want one. Set a Registration Limit and the page shows how many places are left. On a repeating event the limit applies to each date on its own. Free on every plan, with no ceiling on sign-ups.

es_solutions.title: A waitlist and a way to back out
es_solutions.description: A full date shows Join Waitlist. When a guest cancels from the link in their confirmation, the place returns to the count and the next person in line is emailed, with 24 hours to take it. Free on registration events; on priced tickets the waitlist is on Pro.

es_solutions.title: A confirmation that is a ticket
es_solutions.description: Each sign-up gets an email with a QR code and a ticket page of their own, carrying any notes you wrote: directions, parking, what to bring. A reminder follows before the event, a day ahead unless you pick another time. There is no mail merge to run.

es_solutions.title: Payment in the same step
es_solutions.description: On Pro, put a price on a ticket type and guests pay as they book, through your own Stripe or PayPal account, a payment link or cash at the door, among others. Event Schedule adds no platform fee; the processor still charges its own. An order paid online through Stripe or PayPal is marked paid by the payment itself, so there are no two lists to match.

es_solutions.title: A door list that scans
es_solutions.description: Open the Sales page on a phone, press Scan Ticket and point the camera at the code. Each registration admits once and a second scan warns you. Scanning is free and runs in the phone's browser, so it needs a connection. The live check-in dashboard with running counts is on Pro.

es_solutions.title: One link that is the whole event
es_solutions.description: The event page carries the date, the map, the description, the image and the Register button together, with an Add to Calendar menu. It sits on your schedule at your own address beside your other events, so the next sign-up does not start from a blank form.

why_switch.intro: You keep the ten-minute setup. What changes is that a sign-up becomes a place with a holder, a date and a QR code, so the count, the emails and the door all work from the same record.

The confirmation and the reminder, sent without a mail merge

google-forms.switch_lead: Leave past forms where they are. Move the next event, and point the old link at it.

switch_steps.title: Rebuild the next event, not the archive
switch_steps.description: Create a schedule, add the event and choose Free registration on its Tickets tab. Set the Registration Limit to the number your form's response limit stood at. If the form asked extra questions, add them as custom fields on Pro, or keep to name, email and phone on the free plan.

switch_steps.title: Bring across anyone already signed up
switch_steps.description: If the form already has responses, the simplest route is to ask those people to register again from the new link. The attendee import, on Pro, takes a CSV of up to 5,000 rows and can email each person a confirmation, but it files people under a ticket type, so it needs the event set to Sell tickets with a free ticket type, not Free registration.

switch_steps.title: Close the form with a forwarding note
switch_steps.description: Turn off Accepting responses and put the event page address in the message people see on a closed form, so an old link in a chat still leads somewhere. Then share the event link wherever the form link used to go.

faq.question: Can Google Forms limit the number of registrations?
faq.answer: It can limit the number of responses: a form can close itself on a date or after a set number of submissions. What it cannot do is count places: a response for a party of four is one response, a cancellation does not reopen the form, and there is no waitlist. Event Schedule counts one place per registration and per date (with Individual tickets on, each named guest in a party counts), gives a cancelled place back and offers it to the next person waiting.

faq.question: Can I take payment through a Google Form?
faq.answer: Not inside the form: Forms has no payment question. Organizers paste a payment link into the form or its confirmation message and reconcile the two lists afterwards. In Event Schedule a priced ticket is paid during booking through your own Stripe, PayPal or other connected account, which needs Pro at $5 a month. Event Schedule charges no platform fee, and the processor's own fee still applies.

faq.question: What does it cost to move event sign-ups off Google Forms?
faq.answer: Nothing, if the event is free to attend. Registration, the capacity limit, the waitlist on a full registration date, confirmation and reminder emails and door scanning are all on the free plan at $0, with no limit on sign-ups. Pro at $5 a month is for priced tickets, your own questions on the form, the sales export and the live check-in dashboard.

faq.question: Can I ask the same questions I ask in my form?
faq.answer: Name, email and an optional or required phone number are built in on every plan. Your own questions, as text, a dropdown or a yes-or-no, are custom fields and need Pro. There is no file upload question and no branching between sections, so a long application form is still better as a Google Form.

faq.question: Can I keep using Google Forms alongside Event Schedule?
faq.answer: The two sit together well. You can take the sign-up on the event page and still send a Google Form for the things that are not a booking: a volunteer rota, a speaker questionnaire, a catering order. Put the form link in the event description or the registration notes and it reaches everyone who signs up.

faq.question: What does Google Forms still do better?
faq.answer: Long and conditional forms. It has more question types, sections that depend on an answer, file uploads, quizzes, and a linked Sheet that updates live and can be shared with anyone. Event Schedule is not a form builder or a survey tool: it asks a few questions at sign-up and puts its effort into the count, the ticket and the door.

faq.question: How do I move people who already filled in my form?
faq.answer: Download the responses as a CSV from the Responses tab. On Pro you can import that list as attendees of an event that uses ticket types (a free ticket type is enough), up to 5,000 rows at a time. An event on Free registration has no ticket type to import into, so there people register again from the new link. Past events do not need moving: their Sheets stay in your Drive, and you start with the next date.

mailchimp.name: Mailchimp
mailchimp.tagline: New events email your subscribers by themselves and ticket buyers are already a list, within a monthly allowance worth reading before you move.
mailchimp.meta_title: Replace Mailchimp for Event Newsletters | Event Schedule
mailchimp.description: Where Mailchimp stops for event email, what moves to Event Schedule, and the monthly allowance that decides whether your list should stay.
mailchimp.keywords: Mailchimp alternative for events, Mailchimp replacement, event email marketing, event newsletter
mailchimp.audience_hint: For venues, promoters and performers who keep a Mailchimp audience mainly to tell people what is on.
mailchimp.about: Mailchimp is an email marketing service built around an audience of contacts, with tags, segments, signup forms, a campaign builder and automation flows. Event people use it for the monthly what's-on email, the on-sale announcement and the last-tickets push, while the events themselves live somewhere else: a ticketing site, a website calendar or a spreadsheet. It reaches ticketing tools through integrations, such as the one Eventbrite offers.
mailchimp.pricing_note: Mailchimp starts at $13/month for 500 contacts and goes up from there. Event Schedule does not cap subscribers on any plan; what the plan sets is the newsletter allowance, counted in recipients: 10 a month free, 100 on Pro at $5/month, 1,000 on Enterprise. The automatic digest of new events is outside it. Free registration is unlimited, and selling paid tickets is on Pro.

tool_strengths: Automation flows that send a series of emails after a signup, a tag or a date
Tags and segments over one audience, with whatever fields you add to it
A drag-and-drop builder and template library for mail that has nothing to do with events
Lists in the thousands, written to several times a month, on its own sending infrastructure
keep_when: your list is over a thousand people, you write to all of them more than once a month, and you do not want to run your own mail server
you depend on automation flows: a welcome series, a win-back sequence, anything started by a tag or a date
most of what you send is not about events: a shop, a blog, a fundraising appeal, a membership
pain_points: The date moves on the ticketing page on Tuesday. The campaign scheduled for Thursday still says Friday, because the email holds a copy of the event and not the event.
Every what's-on email opens with the same half hour: each event's title, date, price, image and ticket link copied into a content block from wherever it is really kept.
To write only to the people coming on Saturday, you export the order list, import it, tag it and build a segment, on the day you have the least time.
A buyer who never joined the list and a subscriber who never bought sit in two systems, and unless an integration carries them across you cannot tell which is which.
People who unsubscribed keep counting toward the contact limit until you archive them, so the audience on the bill is larger than the one you can write to.
The email can link to an RSVP page but cannot be one: the capacity, the guest list and the door are another tool again.
mailchimp.gaps_lead: Mailchimp sends mail about anything, so it knows nothing about your events in particular. These are the moments where that shows.
mailchimp.gaps_close: None of this is a defect in Mailchimp: it is an email service, and to it an event is text in a campaign like any other text.

today.title: A what's-on email in Mailchimp, start to finish
today.intro: The monthly routine of a venue or promoter whose audience is in Mailchimp and whose events are somewhere else.

steps.title: Collect the addresses
steps.description: A Mailchimp signup form, embedded, hosted or as a pop-up, sits on your website and feeds one audience. Double opt-in is a setting you switch on for that audience. The names from the clipboard at the door are typed in or imported afterwards.

steps.title: Bring the buyers across
steps.description: Ticket buyers are in the ticketing tool. Either its integration copies over the ones who agreed to marketing at checkout, or you export the orders and use Import contacts: upload the file, match the columns, add a tag for the event.

steps.title: Build the campaign
steps.description: Create an email, pick the template, then add a block per event: image, title, date, a button to the ticket page. Each one is copied by hand from the ticketing site or the website calendar.

steps.title: Choose who gets it
steps.description: Send to the whole audience, or build a segment from tags: last season's buyers, the jazz crowd, the people who came to the festival.

steps.title: Test, schedule, send
steps.description: Send yourself a test, fix the button that still points at last month's show, then schedule it. Where your plan has A/B testing, two subject lines go to part of the audience first.

steps.title: After it goes
steps.description: Opens and clicks arrive in the report. If an event then moves or sells out, the sent email stays as it was, and the correction is another campaign.

today.outro: It works, and a great many rooms have been filled this way. The cost is that every event exists twice, once where it is sold and once as text in an email, and you are what keeps the two in step.

mailchimp.native_lead: The same email, written in the place where the events, the buyers and the sign-up form already are.

es_solutions.title: New events announce themselves
es_solutions.description: Publish public events and your confirmed subscribers get one digest listing them, at most one every 72 hours. It is free on every plan and does not come out of the newsletter allowance. You can turn it off per schedule.

es_solutions.title: An Events block that fills itself
es_solutions.description: The Events block lists your events with day, time, price and link, worked out when the newsletter is sent and not when you wrote it. Set a newsletter to repeat on the first of each month, with the Events block set to the rest of that month, and it carries the month's programme without being rebuilt.

es_solutions.title: Buyers are already a segment
es_solutions.description: Ticket buyers is a built-in segment, for every event or for one. Waitlist, sub-schedule, followers and email subscribers are segments too, so writing to Saturday's crowd involves no export.

es_solutions.title: The allowance, stated plainly
es_solutions.description: A newsletter counts every recipient: 10 a month on Free, 100 on Pro, 1,000 on Enterprise, and a send that would go over is refused whole. Connect your own mail server on any plan and the cap comes off, because the mail then leaves through your provider.

es_solutions.title: Sign-up where the events are
es_solutions.description: A sign-up panel on your schedule and event pages, the same form embedded on your own website, a tick box at checkout and a QR code for the door. The panel and the embedded form confirm by email before anyone is added.

es_solutions.title: A/B tests and who opened
es_solutions.description: Try two subject lines, or two openings, on 5 to 50 percent of the list; after the wait you set, the better one goes to everyone else. Each newsletter then shows opens, clicks, failures and unsubscribes. All of it is on the free plan.

why_switch.intro: Move the event mail if your list fits the allowance, or if you will send through your own mail server. If neither is true, keep Mailchimp for the campaigns and let the schedule do the listing, the sign-ups and the tickets.

mailchimp.switch_lead: Count your list against the allowance first, then move the audience, then the form.

switch_steps.title: Export the audience from Mailchimp
switch_steps.description: In Audience, choose Export audience, then Export CSV. The download holds separate files for subscribed, unsubscribed and cleaned contacts. Bring across the subscribed file only, so nobody who opted out hears from you again.

switch_steps.title: Import it and swap the form
switch_steps.description: On the Import Emails tab of Newsletters, upload the CSV, map the email and name columns and save it as a segment. Then take the Mailchimp form off your website and paste in the code from Embed Signup Form on your Followers tab.

switch_steps.title: Send the next what's-on email from here
switch_steps.description: Build it with an Events block and send yourself a test. Review and send shows how many people it reaches and what is left of the month's allowance before anything goes. Say in that email that event news now comes from this address.

faq.question: Is Event Schedule a Mailchimp alternative for event emails?
faq.answer: For telling a small or mid-sized list what is on, it does the job with less copying: events are pulled into the email, buyers are a ready segment, and new events reach subscribers as an automatic digest. It is not a general email marketing tool. There are no drip sequences, no tags and no SMS, and the monthly allowance is small unless you connect your own mail server.

faq.question: How many emails can I send a month, and what does it cost?
faq.answer: The allowance counts recipients, not newsletters: 10 a month on the free plan at $0, 100 on Pro at $5 a month and 1,000 on Enterprise at $15 a month. One newsletter to 300 people uses 300, and a send that would pass the limit is refused whole, never delivered in part. The automatic digest of new events is outside the count. A schedule that sends through its own mail server has no cap on any plan, and neither does a selfhosted install.

faq.question: My list has 5,000 people. Should I switch?
faq.answer: Not for the newsletters, unless you connect your own mail server. The largest hosted allowance is 1,000 newsletter emails a month, each recipient counting as one, so one newsletter to 5,000 people cannot go out on it. With your own SMTP provider entered in the schedule's Email Settings the cap is lifted, and deliverability becomes yours to look after. If that does not appeal, keep Mailchimp for campaigns and use the schedule for event pages, sign-ups and tickets.

faq.question: Can I keep using Mailchimp alongside Event Schedule?
faq.answer: You can, and for a large list it is the sensible arrangement. There is no built-in Mailchimp sync. Every schedule publishes an RSS feed of its upcoming events, and Mailchimp's RSS automation sends from a feed on the schedule you set. On Pro, the Sales page exports orders as a CSV that you can import into your Mailchimp audience.

faq.question: What does Mailchimp still do better?
faq.answer: Automation, list structure and design freedom. Mailchimp has automation flows, tags and custom fields, SMS, and a far larger template library. The newsletter builder here has five designs, a short list of email-safe fonts and no free-form HTML, and a newsletter goes out when you send or schedule it, weekly or monthly repeats included.

faq.question: How do I move my Mailchimp subscribers across?
faq.answer: Export the audience from Mailchimp as a CSV and upload the subscribed file on the Import Emails tab, up to 10,000 addresses at a time on any plan. They land in a segment you can send newsletters to; no account is created for anyone and nobody is added to your followers. Imported addresses do not receive the automatic digest, which goes only to people who signed up on your pages or ticked the box at checkout.

faq.question: Is signing up double opt-in, as it can be in Mailchimp?
faq.answer: On the sign-up panel and the embedded form it always is: a visitor gives a name and an email address and joins only after opening the confirmation link. The tick box at checkout is single opt-in, because the ticket is already being sent to that address. Someone still awaiting confirmation is never emailed.

today.title: A show's graphics in Canva, start to finish
today.intro: One gig at a venue that posts a poster for each night and a line-up for each week.

steps.title: Start from a template
steps.description: Search the templates for a concert poster or event flyer, pick one, swap in the act's photo and type the name, date, door time, venue and price over the placeholder text.

steps.title: Make it yours
steps.description: Apply the Brand Kit if your plan has one, or set the venue's colours and fonts by hand and drop in the logo from your uploads.

steps.title: Resize for each place
steps.description: The poster becomes a square post, a story and a print size. Canva's Resize makes the copies, and from then on each copy is a design of its own to check and keep up to date.

steps.title: Add the way in
steps.description: Paste the ticket link into a QR code from Canva's QR code app and place it in a corner. The same link goes into the caption, which you write in the social app.

steps.title: Download and post
steps.description: Share, then Download: PNG for social, PDF Print for the printer. Upload each file to each account yourself, or schedule it in Content Planner on the plans that include it, one platform per design.

steps.title: Then the weekly line-up
steps.description: Open last week's line-up design, delete seven rows of text and type the next seven from the calendar. When a date changes midweek, every file above is opened again.

today.outro: The first step is design, and Canva is the right place for it. The other five are the same facts retyped, and every retyping is a chance for the image and the event to disagree.

canva.native_lead: Keep the designing where it is. The repeating can come from the events themselves.

es_solutions.title: Dates drawn from the event

Someone pays by bank transfer and the Paid box gets ticked later, from memory. On the night three people say they paid and the column says they did not.
The same person signs up twice under two spellings, and the head count you gave the caterer is high by however many of those there are.
A guest cancels by email. You delete the row, but the list at the door was printed yesterday and their chair is still set.

Protecting the header row prevents accidents, not copying. Google's help says a protected range should not be used as a security measure, and everyone the sheet is shared with can copy every email address in it.
google-sheets.gaps_lead: A sheet is a very good place to keep a list and a poor place to make one. These are the moments the difference shows.
google-sheets.gaps_close: In each of these the spreadsheet is doing what it was made for, which is storing what you type. An event also needs something to act on it.

steps.title: Places counted by formula

steps.title: Payment matched by hand
steps.description: For a paid event a payment link sits in the form or in the confirmation text. The money arrives in another account, and someone ticks Paid row by row against the statement.

steps.title: Confirmations by mail merge

steps.title: The door
steps.description: The list is sorted by surname and printed, or opened on a phone with the Arrived column. Late sign-ups are written at the bottom in pen, and the ticks are typed back into the sheet the next morning.

today.outro: It works, and a great many events run this way. But every join in it is a person: closing the form, matching the payments, sending the merge, reprinting the list. Miss one and the sheet goes on looking correct.

steps.title: Build the registration survey

steps.title: Run the event from the export

steps.title: Send the feedback survey

steps.title: Read the results
steps.description: Analyze gives you a chart per question and an export. Linking a low score to what that person booked, or comparing this month with last, means matching addresses across two surveys and a spreadsheet.

today.outro: The surveys are the quick part. The slow part is carrying the list of people from the first survey to the door, and from the door to the second survey, by export, every time.

Keeping Doodle for the one decision and Event Schedule for everything after it is a sensible split.

faq.question: Does it replace Doodle's Sign-up Sheets and Booking Page?
faq.answer: Sign-up sheets for events, in most cases: free registration gives each date a limit, a waitlist, a QR confirmation and a reminder on the free plan. A sheet of thirty short slots on one evening maps less neatly, since each session would be its own event. For bookable time slots there is appointment booking: one appointment type on the free plan, more types, paid bookings and scheduling rules on Pro, with its emails sent through your schedule's own email settings on eventschedule.com.

faq.question: Can my team mark when they are unavailable?
faq.answer: Only as whole days away. On Enterprise, each member of a talent schedule's team, viewers included, can mark the whole days they are not free, and everyone on the team sees those days on the schedule's calendar. It is a private note with no times and no voting, so it tells a band who is away in August and does not find the evening everyone is free.

faq.question: What does Doodle still do better?
faq.answer: Finding a time. The group poll, voting without an account, scheduling that checks your calendar and invites to everyone who responded are its core, and Event Schedule does not attempt them. Keep Doodle for meetings and for any date that depends on particular people.

faq.question: What does Event Schedule cost for a club or a class?
faq.answer: A schedule, unlimited events, free registration, reminders, calendar sync and the calendar feed are on the free plan at $0. Pro at $5 a month adds priced tickets, event polls and more appointment types. Enterprise at $15 a month adds up to five team members and availability marking.

faq.question: How do I move my existing Doodle polls?
faq.answer: You move their results, not the polls. Add each booked date as an event, or import the dates from the Google Calendar they were booked into, and set each sign-up sheet's seat count as a Registration Limit. Old polls can stay in Doodle as a record.

qr-code-generators.tagline: A generated QR code opens a web address for anyone who scans it. A ticket code belongs to one order and is checked at the door.

qr-code-generators.audience_hint: For organizers who put a QR code on the poster and are wondering whether the same trick can work as a ticket.
qr-code-generators.about: A QR code generator turns a piece of text, usually a web address, into a square image you can print. A static code holds the address in its own pattern, so it cannot be edited once made and keeps working for as long as the address does. A dynamic code holds a short redirect address run by the generator, which lets you change the destination later and count scans. Organizers put them on posters and flyers, and some try to use them as tickets.
qr-code-generators.pricing_note: Many QR generators charge $5 to $15/month for dynamic QR codes. Event Schedule puts a QR code on every ticket and free registration, and scanning them at the door is free on every plan, including tickets you sold before. Pro at $5/month adds the live check-in dashboard.

comparison_rows.feature: A code on a poster that opens a page
A different code for each order
Sends the code to the guest
Knows a code was already used
Checks the order is paid and for this date
Refuses a refunded or cancelled order

comparison_rows.es: A page in the phone browser
Live by ticket type, on Pro

comparison_rows.feature: Colours and a logo in the code

tool_strengths: A static code needs nothing behind it: it has no expiry date and works for as long as the address it holds is online
It is general purpose, so the same tool covers a menu, a sign-up form and a poster that opens your event page
A dynamic code can be pointed somewhere new after the poster is printed, and reports how often it was scanned
Many generators let you set colours and place a logo in the code for print
keep_when: the code only has to open a page: a poster, a table card, the last slide of a talk
you want a styled code with your logo and colours, which Event Schedule does not make
the event is open to all, and nobody is counted or turned away at the door
pain_points: You make one code and print it on every ticket. At the door it scans, and so does the copy a guest forwarded to four friends, because the code only holds an address.

To make tickets unique you generate a code per guest, name the files and attach each to the right email. At forty guests that is an evening, and one swapped file sends a stranger someone else's ticket.
The volunteer on the door scans a code with the phone camera and a web page opens. Nothing says whether this person paid, and nothing is written down, so the second scan looks exactly like the first.
Two doors, two volunteers, one printed list. Both tick off the same forwarded ticket a minute apart, and neither can know.
A guest was refunded on Tuesday. Their code still scans on Saturday, because a printed pattern cannot be told about a refund.
The dynamic code on five hundred posters runs through the generator's redirect. If that redirect stops working, the posters lead nowhere.
qr-code-generators.gaps_lead: A QR code is a way of writing an address so that a camera can read it. A ticket needs something a picture cannot hold: a record of whether it has been used.
qr-code-generators.gaps_close: A generator does what it says, and for a poster that is all you need. Being a ticket was never its job.

today.title: A door run on generated QR codes
today.intro: There are two versions of this job. The code on the poster works. The code as a ticket is where the evenings go.

steps.title: Make the poster code
steps.description: Paste the address of your event page or sign-up form into a generator and download the image. A static code is fixed from that moment, so a typo in the address means a new code and a reprint.

steps.title: Take sign-ups somewhere else
steps.description: The code only opens a page. Names and payments are collected by a form, a payment link or a ticketing site, and the generator never learns who signed up.

steps.title: Decide what the ticket code holds
steps.description: Either every guest gets the same code, which proves nothing, or you invent a value per guest, such as an order number, and make a code for each. Some generators take a spreadsheet and produce them in bulk.

steps.title: Send each guest their code
steps.description: The right image goes into the right email, by mail merge or by hand. When a guest loses theirs, you find the file and send it again.

steps.title: Scan at the door with the camera
steps.description: A phone camera reads the code and shows its value or opens its link. A person then finds that value on the list and marks it used, because the camera checks nothing.

steps.title: Reconcile the next morning
steps.description: Attendance is whatever was ticked on the sheet. Duplicates, refunds and people who paid at the door are sorted out from memory.

today.outro: The generator finished its part in step one. Everything after that is a verification system built by hand from a spreadsheet, a mail merge and a volunteer's eyesight.

qr-code-generators.native_lead: Here the code is issued with the order, and the record behind it decides who gets in.

es_solutions.title: A code issued with every order
es_solutions.description: When someone registers or buys, the confirmation email and their ticket page carry a QR code that belongs to that order alone. Free registrations get one too, on every plan. Nobody generates, names or attaches a file.

es_solutions.title: A scanner that checks, not only reads
es_solutions.description: Open Scan Ticket on a phone and point the camera. The answer comes back green, amber or red with the name on the order; the first scan admits, and a second says already checked in and when. Free on every plan. It is a page in the browser, not an app, and each scan needs a connection.

es_solutions.title: Refunds and wrong nights are caught
es_solutions.description: The scanner asks the server whether the order is paid, for this event and for tonight. A cancelled or refunded order is refused, and a ticket for another date stops in amber so that a person decides.

es_solutions.title: A running count, on Pro
es_solutions.description: The check-in dashboard shows how many people are in, broken down by ticket type, and finds a guest by name or email. That dashboard is the Pro part of check-in. Scanning itself has no plan attached.

es_solutions.title: The poster code is covered too
es_solutions.description: Each schedule has a QR code to download on every plan, which opens the schedule with its sign-up form ready, and the events graphic prints a code on each flyer that leads to that event's page. They are plain codes. For one with your logo in it, a generator is still the right tool.

es_solutions.title: Guest lists and comps get codes
es_solutions.description: On Pro, import a guest list from a CSV file or type it in, up to 5,000 rows at a time, and each person can be emailed a confirmation with a code of their own. Tickets with a price are also on Pro, with no platform fee; the payment processor charges its own.

why_switch.intro: Nothing you made in a generator has to be thrown away. The poster code keeps pointing where it points. What changes is that the ticket stops being a picture you made and becomes a record the door can ask.
points: The poster code: keep it if the address behind it still leads somewhere useful, or make a new one for the event page
Your guest list, typed in or imported from CSV on Pro, with a code for each row
The door: the same phones, opening a scanner page in place of the camera app
The tally: checked in or not is recorded per order at the moment of the scan
Free sign-ups, which get a code and a place on the list on every plan

qr-code-generators.switch_lead: Start with the next event that has a door.

switch_steps.title: Put the event on a schedule
switch_steps.description: Create the event and turn on free registration with a limit, or ticket types with a price on Pro. From then on, every sign-up is emailed a code of its own.

switch_steps.title: Repoint or reprint the poster code
switch_steps.description: A dynamic code can be edited in your generator to open the new event page. A static one cannot, so keep the old page online with a link across, or make a new code from the event address for the next print run.

switch_steps.title: Rehearse the door once
switch_steps.description: Register yourself, sign in on the door phone, open Sales and tap Scan Ticket where the door will be. Check there is signal or wifi, and tell guests that the code in their confirmation email is the ticket.

faq.question: Can I use a free QR code generator to make event tickets?
faq.answer: You can make the codes, but not the check. A generator hands you an image; knowing that a code belongs to a paid order and has not been used takes a record that every scan is compared with. Without one, a screenshot of a single ticket admits as many people as receive it.

faq.question: What is the difference between a QR code on a poster and a QR code on a ticket?
faq.answer: A poster code is the same for everyone and opens a page. A ticket code belongs to one order and is looked up when scanned: is it paid, is it for this event and date, has it been used. The first is a link, and the second is a key to a record.

faq.question: Do I still need a QR code generator if I use Event Schedule?
faq.answer: Not for tickets, since a code is issued with each registration or sale. For print you may still want one. Event Schedule gives each schedule a plain QR image to download, and a generator is the better tool for a code in your colours with a logo, or one that points at something other than your schedule.

faq.question: What does scanning tickets cost?
faq.answer: Scanning tickets and free registrations at the door is on the Free plan, at $0. Putting a price on a ticket, the live check-in dashboard and importing a guest list are on Pro at $5 a month. No platform fee is taken on ticket sales on any plan; the payment processor still charges its own fee.

faq.question: Do door staff need an app or a scanner gun?
faq.answer: Neither: the scanner is a page in the phone browser that uses the camera. It needs a connection for every scan, because each one is checked against a single shared record, and there is no offline mode. Door staff with a sign-in of their own are team members, which is Enterprise, up to five people.

faq.question: What happens when someone shows a screenshot of another person's ticket?
faq.answer: The first scan of that code admits the order. The next scan, from any phone at any door, shows already checked in with the time of the first one, and the person on the door decides what to do. A screenshot is fine for the real guest, and it opens with no signal.

faq.question: I already sent out codes from a generator. Can I move those guests across?
faq.answer: The old codes cannot be brought in, because they are images with no order behind them. The guests can: on Pro, import the list from CSV onto an event with ticket types, with Send Email on, and each person imported as paid receives a confirmation with a code that scans. Tell them the new email replaces the old one.

Its calendar page, called an events page on version 7.0 sites, shows events as a list or a month, and each event has a title, a start and end time, a location with a map pin, an excerpt and a featured image. Organizers use it as the What's On page of their site and add registration with a form, a service product or an outside ticketing service.

tool_strengths: The whole site in one place: home page, about, blog, shop and events share one design and one navigation
Layout freedom: an event description is built from blocks, so it can hold a gallery, a video, a form or a product
Calendar and summary blocks that show upcoming events on the home page or any other page
Built-in commerce, so a workshop can be sold as a service product with its stock as the capacity
keep_when: you host a handful of one-off events a year, and a title, a date and a paragraph is all each one needs
events are a small corner of a site that mainly sells products, shows a portfolio or runs a blog
you want every event page laid out by hand, differently each time
pain_points: Your Thursday open mic runs every week. Calendar pages have no repeating events, so each Thursday is a duplicate you make and re-date by hand, and a new start time is an edit to every copy.
A workshop is sold as a service product with stock set to the number of places. That is a product to create beside every event, with a matching title and the date typed into its name.
The buyer of that product has a shop order, not a ticket. At the door you work down the orders list on a laptop, with nothing to scan.
For a ticketed show you send people to Eventbrite or Tock and list the event on the calendar page as well. Each event now lives in two systems, and a changed date has to be changed in both.
A free talk needs a headcount, so a form goes into the event description. The sign-ups arrive as form submissions, apart from the event, and someone has to keep count.
The day you want to move, the events are the part that stays behind: Squarespace's site export does not include calendar pages.
squarespace.gaps_lead: A calendar page is a list of dated entries. It shows an event well and stops there: repeating it, counting places, issuing a ticket and checking it at the door fall to other blocks and other services.
squarespace.gaps_close: Squarespace says as much in its own help pages, which send bookings to Acuity Scheduling and tickets to Tock or Eventbrite. It is a website builder doing what a website builder does.

today.title: Events on a Squarespace site, start to finish
today.intro: Most Squarespace sites that list events are run the same way, by whoever also looks after everything else on the site.

steps.title: Add a calendar page
steps.description: It becomes the What's On page. You choose the list or the month view; on a version 7.0 site the same thing is called an events page.

steps.title: Enter each event
steps.description: Title, start and end time (an end time is required), the address, which drops a pin on a map, an excerpt and a featured image. The featured image is the thumbnail only, so the poster goes in a second time as an image block in the description.

steps.title: Duplicate for every repeat
steps.description: There is no repeating event. For a weekly class you open the event's menu, choose Duplicate and change the date, once for each week you want listed.

steps.title: Bolt on a way to sign up
steps.description: For a paid workshop, Squarespace's own guide is a service product per session, stock set to the number of places, and a product block in the event description. For ticketed events it points to Tock or Eventbrite, with a link from the event.

steps.title: Turn on the calendar links
steps.description: Show Export Links adds Google Calendar and iCal links to each event. Times are shown in the site's time zone.

steps.title: Run the night from a list
steps.description: Who is coming is a list of shop orders, form submissions or the other service's attendee report. Afterwards the event drops into past events, and the product behind it stays in the store until you take it down.

today.outro: The page looks right, because Squarespace is good at pages. The event itself is spread over a calendar entry, a product or an outside ticket page, and whichever list you check names against.

squarespace.native_lead: The site stays where it is. The events move to a schedule that sits inside it.

es_solutions.title: An event page with nothing to assemble
es_solutions.description: Enter the event once and its page has the flyer, the date and time, the venue with a map, add to calendar buttons and a register or buy button. Free on every plan. On the Free plan the public pages carry Event Schedule branding, which Pro removes.

es_solutions.title: A weekly night is one event
es_solutions.description: A recurring event repeats daily, weekly on chosen days, every few weeks, monthly or yearly, with single dates added or skipped. You edit the series, not fifty-two copies. Free on every plan.

es_solutions.title: Sign-ups and tickets on the event itself
es_solutions.description: Free registration counts places against a limit for each date and is unlimited on every plan. Ticket types with a price are on Pro, paid into your own Stripe, PayPal or other connected account with no platform fee; the processor still charges its own. There is no product to keep in step with the event.

es_solutions.title: The calendar goes in a Code block
es_solutions.description: Copy the Iframe Code from the Embed dialog and paste it into a Code block on your Squarespace page. On the Free plan the snippet carries a small Powered by Event Schedule line under the frame. It shows your live schedule, so a date you move is already right on the site. The calendar embed is free; the widget that sells tickets inside your page is on Pro. Which Squarespace plans allow an iframe in a Code block is Squarespace's decision, so check yours.

es_solutions.title: A ticket that scans
es_solutions.description: Each registration and each ticket is emailed with a QR code of its own. A phone browser scans it at the door on any plan, and an order admits once. The live check-in dashboard is on Pro.

es_solutions.title: Your look, within limits
es_solutions.description: Colours, fonts, backgrounds and a header image are free. Custom CSS and removing Event Schedule branding are on Pro, and your own domain, such as events.yourdomain.com, is on Enterprise. It is not a page builder: there are no free-form layouts, and no blog or shop.

why_switch.intro: You are not replacing the website. You are replacing the calendar page and the workarounds hung off it, and leaving the home page, the blog and the shop exactly where they are.

squarespace.switch_lead: Nothing imports from a calendar page, so move forward from the next date and leave the archive where it is.

switch_steps.title: Re-enter what is coming up
switch_steps.description: Squarespace's export leaves calendar pages out, so copy each upcoming event across by hand, or paste its page link into the import and check what was read. Make each repeating event once, as a series.

switch_steps.title: Swap the calendar page for the embed
switch_steps.description: On your What's On page, put a Code block holding the iframe tag from the Embed dialog where the event list was. Keep the page address and the navigation label, so links and search results still land there. The old calendar page can move to Not linked if you want to keep the archive.

switch_steps.title: Retire the stand-ins
switch_steps.description: Once their dates have passed, unpublish the service products that stood in for workshop places and remove the sign-up forms. Tell your list that sign-up now happens on the event page and that the confirmation email is the ticket.

faq.question: Can I keep my Squarespace site and move only the events?
faq.answer: That works. The site stays on Squarespace, and the calendar goes into a Code block as an iframe that shows your live schedule. A click on an event opens its page in a new tab, where people register or buy.

faq.question: Does Squarespace have recurring events?
faq.answer: Not on calendar pages: its help centre says repeating events are not supported and suggests duplicating an event instead. On Event Schedule a recurring event is one entry that repeats daily, weekly, monthly or yearly, with single dates added or skipped, on every plan.

faq.question: How do people sell event tickets on Squarespace today?
faq.answer: By one of two routes. For workshops, Squarespace's guide is a service product for each session, with stock as the capacity and a product block in the event description. For ticketed events it suggests Tock or Eventbrite, with the event promoted on a calendar page. Either way the ticket and the event are separate things to keep in step.

faq.question: Is Event Schedule a website builder?
faq.answer: No. It gives you a schedule page, a page for each event and a calendar you can embed, and that is the extent of it: no free-form pages, no blog, no shop. If you need a full site, keep Squarespace for that and use the schedule for the events part.

faq.question: What does it cost on top of a Squarespace plan?
faq.answer: If you keep the site it is an addition, not a swap. Event pages, the calendar embed, recurring events, free registration and door scanning are on the Free plan at $0. Tickets with a price, the ticket widget and pages without our branding are on Pro at $5 a month, and a custom domain is on Enterprise at $15 a month. No platform fee is taken on sales; your payment processor charges its own.

faq.question: What does Squarespace still do better?
faq.answer: Design, and everything that is not an event. You lay out each page block by block, and the events sit in the same navigation and style as the rest of the site. An embedded calendar is a frame whose height you set yourself, and it arrives in the schedule's own colours and fonts, which you match to the site by hand.

faq.question: Can my existing Squarespace events be imported?
faq.answer: There is no importer for a calendar page, and Squarespace's own site export does not include calendar pages. Upcoming events are entered again: paste an event's text or its link and the details are read for you, within a daily limit, then check them. Moving only the coming dates, and leaving past events on the old page, is the short route.

steps.description: A Calendar view for the month, a List or Gallery view filtered to upcoming dates, sometimes a Board by type. A filter on Status keeps anything not yet confirmed out of sight, which is how drafts are handled.

steps.title: Publish
steps.description: Share, then Publish. The page and all of its subpages go live, visitors can switch between the views and open each event, and the Discoverable on the web toggle decides whether search engines may list it.

steps.title: Sign-ups through a form
steps.description: A form connected to a Registrations database, open to anyone on the web with the link, with a question that says which event. Answers land in its Responses view. Registration closes when you set the form to No access.

steps.title: Money and tickets elsewhere
steps.description: For a paid event the URL property points at a payment link or a ticketing site. Who paid is checked over there and, on a careful day, copied back into the row.

steps.title: Telling people
steps.description: The page link goes in the bio. The published page sends nothing, so each new event is announced by hand in whatever channel you use, and a changed date is announced a second time.

today.outro: The result looks good. It is also a brochure: whatever a visitor does after reading it happens in another tool, and the join between the two is you.

notion.native_lead: The same public calendar, with the buttons the visitor was looking for.

es_solutions.title: A calendar made for visitors
es_solutions.description: Your schedule is a public calendar at its own address, with a month view, a list, and a panel to search and filter. Each event has a page that sets out its date, venue, image and description. Free, with unlimited events.

es_solutions.title: Register on the event page
es_solutions.description: Free registration sits on the event itself, with an optional capacity that closes sign-up at your number and a waitlist behind it. Unlimited on every plan. Adding your own questions to the form is on Pro.

es_solutions.title: Into their calendar, and yours
es_solutions.description: A visitor adds one event to their calendar or subscribes to the schedule's live feed, which follows a date when it moves. On your side, two-way sync with Google Calendar, Outlook and CalDAV is free and is set up by the schedule's owner.

es_solutions.title: Read in, not retyped
es_solutions.description: Paste the rows of your Events database, or a screenshot of its calendar view, into the import box. The events come back as a list with name, date, venue and description filled in, and you tick the ones to add. On Free and Pro a schedule gets 50 of these reads a day.

es_solutions.title: New events announce themselves
es_solutions.description: Visitors follow the schedule or leave an email address, and confirmed subscribers get an automatic digest when you publish new events. For anything else there is a newsletter builder, whose monthly allowance counts recipients: 10 on Free, 100 on Pro, 1,000 on Enterprise.

es_solutions.title: Sub-schedules for filtered views
es_solutions.description: Split one schedule into strands such as Workshops, Socials and Talks. A sub-schedule has a color, an address of its own and a filter button on the calendar. It sorts events and never hides them: a draft is hidden by the event's own visibility.

why_switch.intro: Leave the wiki where it is. The part that moves is the page the public sees, and it moves without being rebuilt row by row.
points: The Events database: pasted in as text or a screenshot, and reviewed before anything is added
The filtered views: sub-schedules, categories and the visitor's own filter panel
The sign-up form: free registration with a capacity, on the event page
The repeating template: one recurring event with a rule such as the 2nd Tuesday, with single dates added or skipped
The link in your bio: one schedule address, or your own domain on Enterprise

notion.switch_lead: The database can stay in Notion as your planning record. Only the published half changes address.

switch_steps.title: Take the upcoming rows out
switch_steps.description: Filter a table view to upcoming events and export it as Markdown and CSV from the page menu. Paste the contents of the CSV into the import box on a free schedule, up to 10,000 characters at a time. Events come back as a list to tick, and nothing is public until you add it.

switch_steps.title: Turn views into sub-schedules
switch_steps.description: Make a sub-schedule or a category for each Select value you used to filter by. Switch on registration for the events that had a form and set the capacity. For a paid event, add a priced ticket on Pro in place of the payment link.

switch_steps.title: Point the old page at the new one
switch_steps.description: Replace the published database with a line of text and a link to your schedule, or unpublish it, and change the link in your bio. Tell your audience they can now follow the schedule or subscribe to its calendar, which the old page had no way to offer.

faq.question: Can I keep planning in Notion and publish with Event Schedule?
faq.answer: That split works well. Notion keeps the tasks, documents and budgets, and Event Schedule carries the public calendar, registration and tickets. On Pro the REST API and webhooks let a script or an automation tool write a sale or a new event back to a Notion database, though there is no ready-made Notion connector.

faq.question: What does Notion still do better?
faq.answer: The whole planning side. Event Schedule has no documents, no task lists and no relations between databases, and custom fields on events are a Pro feature. A Notion page can also be laid out however you like, where an event page here keeps one structure and takes your accent color, font and images.

faq.question: Can visitors add my events to Google Calendar from a published Notion page?
faq.answer: Not from the published page. Notion's help says a database can be viewed in Notion Calendar and not in Google or iCloud calendar. On Event Schedule an event page has an Add to Calendar menu, and the schedule has a live feed that a calendar app can subscribe to.

faq.question: How do I move my events out of a Notion database?
faq.answer: Export the view as CSV and paste its contents into the import box, or add a screenshot of the view. One read can return several events for review, and nothing is added until you tick it. The longer notes inside each page stay in Notion, which is usually where they belong.

faq.question: Do I pay for each team member?
faq.answer: No plan is priced by the seat. Free is $0 with one login per schedule, Pro is $5 a month and adds priced tickets, and Enterprise is $15 a month and carries up to five team members as admins or viewers. If more than five people edit your Notion database today, that ceiling is the thing to weigh.

faq.question: Can I hide draft events the way a filtered view does?
faq.answer: Every plan has two states, Public and Draft, and a draft is seen only by the schedule's own people. Unlisted events, reached by a direct link with an optional password, and Internal events for the team are on Enterprise. A sub-schedule is not a way to hide anything.

faq.question: Can I put the calendar on my own website?
faq.answer: The snippet from the Embed dialog places the live calendar on a site that accepts an iframe, free on every plan, and it updates when your events change. The ticket purchase form can be embedded as well, on Pro.

trello.name: Trello
trello.tagline: A card can plan an event. It cannot publish it, take a registration for it or sell a ticket to it.
trello.meta_title: Replace Trello for Event Management | Event Schedule
trello.description: How events are run as cards on a Trello board, where the board stops at the public, and what to move off it without giving up the planning.
trello.keywords: Trello alternative for events, Trello replacement, Trello event planning, event management board
trello.audience_hint: For venue bookers, promoters and committees who track each event as a card moving from Ideas to Confirmed to Done.
trello.about: Trello is a kanban board: lists from left to right, and cards that move between them. Event teams tend to keep one card per event, with a due date for the night and a checklist of everything to do before it, or one board for a large event with a card per task. It is a planning tool and a good one. Event Schedule is not a planning tool: it has no tasks, no checklists and no board.
trello.pricing_note: Trello Standard costs $5 per user a month billed annually ($6 monthly). Event Schedule is free for unlimited events and public pages. Free registration is unlimited, and selling paid tickets is on Pro at $5/month, and nothing here is charged per user; a team of five is the Enterprise plan rather than five subscriptions.

comparison_rows.feature: Tasks and checklists before the event

comparison_rows.es: QR scan in a phone browser

tool_strengths: The whole season on one screen: a list per stage, a card per event, and dragging the card is the status update
A checklist inside each card for the jobs before the night, and template cards so every new event starts from the same one
Automation and Power-Ups that move cards and connect other tools without anyone writing code
A Calendar Power-Up that sets cards with due dates on a week or a month, with an iCalendar feed for your own calendar app
keep_when: the work is the preparation: booking the room, chasing the rider, ordering the banner
the event is internal, and nobody outside the team has to find it, sign up or pay
a large event wants a board to itself with a card per task. Keep that board, and publish the event from a schedule
pain_points: The card reaches Confirmed and nothing happens outside the board. Someone still writes the event up for the website, the socials and the ticket page, copying the date off the card each time.
You make the board public so people can see what is on. They get lists to scroll through, and Trello's help says public boards are not indexed by search engines, so nobody arrives by searching.
The due date stands in for the show. Start date and duration are only available within Trello, so in an outside calendar the night arrives as a single moment with no end.
The band emails a later start. You change the card. The website, the ticket page and the poster still say eight.
A card has no place for a stranger to register, so sign-up is a link in the description to some other form, and the head count comes back to the board only if someone types it into a comment.
After the night the card is dragged to Done and archived. It was the only record of the event, and it never held a list of who came.
trello.gaps_lead: A board tracks work your team does. An event also has an audience, and the audience never sees the board.
trello.gaps_close: Trello makes no claim to be a box office or a listings page. It is a board for work, and the public half of an event sits outside it.

today.title: An event on a Trello board, from card to doors
today.intro: One card per event is the common setup for a venue or a series. This is the life of that card.

steps.title: A card in Ideas
steps.description: Someone adds a card with the act or a working title. It gathers comments, a few links and a rough month.

steps.title: A date and a checklist
steps.description: Once the night is agreed the card gets a due date and a checklist from the template card: contract, deposit, artwork, listing, tickets, sound check. The date is set by hand, since a template card does not carry dates over. The card moves to Confirmed.

steps.title: The calendar
steps.description: With the Calendar Power-Up enabled, dated cards sit on a month grid, and its iCalendar feed shows those due dates in the team's own calendar apps. It is the nearest the board comes to a program of events, and only the team sees it.

steps.title: Publishing by copy and paste
steps.description: Three of the checklist items are really publishing: write the listing, open the tickets, post the graphic. Each is done in a different tool, with the title, date and price retyped from the card.

steps.title: Changes
steps.description: When something moves, the card is edited first and the checklist grows: update the website, update the ticket page, tell the buyers. Whether those happen depends on who opens the card.

steps.title: Doors, then Done
steps.description: On the night the guest list comes from wherever the tickets were sold. Next morning the card is dragged to Done.

today.outro: The board knew everything about the event and could tell nobody outside the team. Each public fact was copied out of a card by hand, and each change had to be copied out again.

trello.native_lead: What the Confirmed list was waiting for: the event published once, in the place the public and the calendars read it from.

es_solutions.title: Confirmed means published
es_solutions.description: Add the event to your schedule and it has a public page and a square on your calendar. Hold it as a Draft until the contract is signed, then set it to Public. Events are unlimited on the free plan.

es_solutions.title: Registration and tickets on the event
es_solutions.description: Free registration with a capacity limit is on every plan. Priced tickets are on Pro, paid through your own Stripe, PayPal, Payfast, Razorpay or Invoice Ninja account, a payment link or cash. Event Schedule adds no platform fee, and the processor's own fee still applies.

es_solutions.title: One edit, every copy
es_solutions.description: Change the start time on the event and the page, the calendar embedded on your website, the feed people subscribed to and a connected Google, Outlook or CalDAV calendar carry the new time. Two-way sync is free, and the schedule's owner sets it up.

es_solutions.title: A queue for incoming events
es_solutions.description: Turn on Accept requests and bands, promoters or neighbors send an event through a public form. Each waits on the Requests tab until you accept or decline it: an Ideas list where the person asking does the typing. Free, and your own questions on the form are on Pro.

es_solutions.title: A guest list that exists
es_solutions.description: Each registration and sale is on the Sales page, and each ticket carries a QR code read at the door from a phone browser, free on every plan. The live check-in dashboard is on Pro. The morning after, you know who came.

es_solutions.title: A team, at one plan
es_solutions.description: Free and Pro have a single login per schedule. Enterprise carries up to five team members: an admin adds events, answers requests and sees sales, and a viewer browses the calendar and scans tickets. Nothing is priced by the seat.

why_switch.intro: Nothing about the board has to change. What goes away is the copying between the board and the outside world.
points: Dated cards: read in as events from pasted text, a screenshot of the board or a calendar feed, and reviewed before any is added
The "write the listing" item: the event page is the listing
The "open the tickets" item: registration or tickets on that same page
The "post the graphic" item: a shareable image of upcoming events, generated from the schedule on every plan
The update chores after a change: one edit, carried to the page, the embed, the feed and the synced calendar

trello.switch_lead: Start with the Confirmed list. An idea can stay a card until it is real.

switch_steps.title: Read the Confirmed list in
switch_steps.description: If the board uses the Calendar Power-Up, copy its iCalendar feed address and paste it on the import page of a free schedule: a calendar link is read directly, and upcoming entries come back as a list to tick. Otherwise paste the card titles and dates as text, or add a screenshot. Check every time, because a due date has no end.

switch_steps.title: Shorten the template checklist
switch_steps.description: Swap the listing, ticket and graphic items on your template card for one: publish on the schedule. When the event page exists, put its link on the card, so the board points at the public version and stops being the source of it.

switch_steps.title: Change the public links
switch_steps.description: If a public board was how people saw what is on, put your schedule address in its place and embed the calendar on your website. Tell your audience they can follow the schedule or subscribe to its calendar feed, which a board never gave them.

faq.question: Can I keep using Trello alongside Event Schedule?
faq.answer: Running both is the sensible setup. Trello holds the tasks, and Event Schedule holds the published event, the registrations and the tickets. On Pro, webhooks fire on sales, events and check-ins and the REST API can create events, so an automation tool or a short script can tie a card to its event. There is no ready-made Trello Power-Up.

faq.question: What does Trello still do better?
faq.answer: Planning. Event Schedule has no boards, no task cards, no checklists and nobody to assign a job to. It does not manage volunteers, speakers or exhibitors either. When the hard part of your event is the preparation, that work stays on the board.

faq.question: Does Event Schedule have a kanban or pipeline view of events?
faq.answer: No. Events appear on a calendar and in lists, and every plan has two states for them, Draft and Public. The nearest thing to a pipeline is the Requests tab, where submitted events wait until you accept or decline each one.

faq.question: How do I get my events off the board and onto a schedule?
faq.answer: Paste them. The import box reads pasted text, an image such as a screenshot of the board, or a link to a calendar feed, and returns the events as a list for you to review. One link read brings back up to 100 events, and an import can be undone for 24 hours.

faq.question: What does it cost compared with paying per member?
faq.answer: Plans are flat. Free is $0, Pro is $5 a month for priced tickets and the API, and Enterprise is $15 a month for up to five team members and your own domain. The catch for a large team is that five is the ceiling. Ticket sales carry no platform fee, only the payment processor's.

faq.question: Can my whole committee see the events in their own calendars?
faq.answer: Anyone can subscribe to the schedule's public calendar feed without an account, so a committee of any size can follow what is published. Team members on Enterprise can also send the schedule's events to a Google calendar of their own. It is editing that is limited to the team.

faq.question: Can performers or partners send me events the way they would add a card?
faq.answer: With Accept requests on, anyone can submit an event from your schedule page without being invited to a board. By default each submission waits for your approval, and schedules you name as approved skip the queue. This is free on every plan; adding your own questions to the form needs Pro.
